The text studies the representation theory of a semidirect product \(GV\), where \(G\) is a finite group and \(V\) is a finite \(G\)-module. In this setting, \(V\) is viewed as a normal subgroup of \(GV\), and the action of \(G\) on \(V\) determines the structure of the semidirect product.

The main focus is on obtaining upper bounds for the sizes of certain subsets of \(\Irr(GV)\), the set of irreducible complex characters of \(GV\). Rather than estimating the total number of irreducible characters directly, the text considers more refined collections of characters defined by their behavior on particular subgroups of \(V\).

One important subset consists of those irreducible characters \(\chi \in \Irr(GV)\) whose restriction to the cyclic subgroup \(\langle v\rangle\), generated by a fixed element \(v \in V\), is not a multiple of the regular character of \(\langle v\rangle\). In other words, these are the characters whose values on \(\langle v\rangle\) fail to exhibit the uniform behavior expected from a direct sum of copies of the regular representation. Bounding the size of this subset gives information about how many irreducible characters of \(GV\) behave exceptionally with respect to the element \(v\).

The results provide quantitative estimates for such exceptional sets of irreducible characters. These estimates are relevant because questions about the number of conjugacy classes, or equivalently the number of irreducible characters, of semidirect products \(GV\) play an important role in finite group theory.

In particular, the bounds may be useful for studying the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem. This problem concerns the number \(k(GV)\) of conjugacy classes of \(GV\), especially in situations where the orders of \(G\) and \(V\) are not coprime. The coprime case has been extensively studied, but the non-coprime setting presents additional difficulties. By controlling the number of irreducible characters with certain exceptional restrictions to subgroups of \(V\), the text offers tools that may contribute to progress on this broader problem.

This text investigates the representation theory of semidirect products \(GV\), where a finite group \(G\) acts on a finite module \(V\). In particular, it focuses on the irreducible complex characters of \(GV\) and on how these characters behave when restricted to certain subgroups generated by elements of the module \(V\). The central idea is that information about restrictions to cyclic subgroups \(\langle v\rangle\), with \(v \in V\), can be used to control and estimate the size of distinguished subsets of \(\operatorname{Irr}(GV)\), the set of irreducible characters of \(GV\).

The motivation for this study comes from the broader \(k(GV)\)-problem, which asks for bounds on the number of conjugacy classes, or equivalently the number of irreducible characters, of a semidirect product \(GV\). In the classical coprime setting, where \(|G|\) and \(|V|\) are relatively prime, strong results are known. However, the non-coprime case remains much more difficult. Since the equality \(k(GV)=|\operatorname{Irr}(GV)|\) connects conjugacy class counts with character theory, estimates for families of irreducible characters can provide useful tools for approaching this problem.

The text develops upper bounds for the sizes of certain subsets of \(\operatorname{Irr}(GV)\). These subsets are defined by conditions involving the restriction of irreducible characters of \(GV\) to cyclic subgroups of \(V\). More precisely, for elements \(v\in V\), one studies the multiplicities and constituents appearing in the restriction of characters to \(\langle v\rangle\). By analyzing how often a given type of restriction can occur, the paper obtains quantitative bounds that depend on the structure of the action of \(G\) on \(V\) and on the behavior of elements of \(V\) under this action.

A key feature of the argument is that it does not require the action of \(G\) on \(V\) to be coprime. This is significant because many of the standard tools available in coprime representation theory are no longer directly applicable in the non-coprime setting. Instead, the approach uses character-theoretic restrictions and orbit-counting ideas to extract information from the module structure itself. The resulting estimates give a way to limit the number of irreducible characters that can satisfy certain prescribed restriction properties.

The main theorem establishes explicit upper bounds for these subsets of irreducible characters of \(GV\). While the result does not by itself settle the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem, it supplies bounds that may be useful in future work on the problem. By relating irreducible characters of the full semidirect product to their behavior on small cyclic subgroups of the module, the text provides a method for reducing global questions about \(GV\) to more local questions involving elements of \(V\) and their stabilizers under the action of \(G\).

Overall, the work contributes to the study of finite group actions on modules and the character theory of semidirect products. Its main contribution is a set of upper bounds for selected families of irreducible characters, obtained through restrictions to cyclic subgroups generated by module elements. These bounds offer a potential tool for further progress on the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem and related questions concerning the number of conjugacy classes and irreducible characters in semidirect products.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal mathematical language, state the main contribution of a paper concerning finite groups \(G\), finite \(G\)-modules \(V\), irreducible characters of \(GV\), and possible applications to the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem.
counterfactuals.output:
A formal statement of the main contribution can be phrased as follows.

Let \(G\) be a finite group and let \(V\) be a finite \(G\)-module, written additively, so that one may form the semidirect product

\[
GV:=G\ltimes V .
\]

Let \(\operatorname{Irr}(X)\) denote the set of ordinary irreducible complex characters of a finite group \(X\), and let \(k(X)=|\operatorname{Irr}(X)|\) be the number of conjugacy classes of \(X\). Let \(G\) act naturally on the dual group

\[
\widehat V=\operatorname{Irr}(V),
\]

and for \(\lambda\in \widehat V\), let

\[
G_\lambda=\{g\in G\mid \lambda^g=\lambda\}
\]

be its stabilizer.

The main contribution is the use of Clifford theory to describe the irreducible characters of \(GV\) in terms of the stabilizers of linear characters of \(V\). Namely, if \(\Lambda\subseteq \widehat V\) is a set of representatives for the \(G\)-orbits on \(\widehat V\), then there is a natural parametrization

\[
\operatorname{Irr}(GV)
\;\longleftrightarrow\;
\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in \Lambda} \operatorname{Irr}(G_\lambda).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
k(GV)
=
\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda} k(G_\lambda).
\]

Here each \(\lambda\in \operatorname{Irr}(V)\) extends to \(G_\lambda V\) by letting \(G_\lambda\) act trivially, and the corresponding irreducible characters of \(GV\) are obtained by induction:

\[
\chi_{\lambda,\theta}
=
\operatorname{Ind}_{G_\lambda V}^{GV}(\widehat\lambda\,\theta),
\qquad
\theta\in \operatorname{Irr}(G_\lambda).
\]

Thus every irreducible character of \(GV\) arises uniquely in this way, up to \(G\)-conjugacy of \(\lambda\).

In the context of the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem, this reduces the desired inequality

\[
k(GV)\leq |V|
\]

to the problem of estimating the sum

\[
\sum_{\lambda\in \Lambda} k(G_\lambda)
\]

without assuming \((|G|,|V|)=1\). Therefore, the contribution provides a character-theoretic framework for attacking the non-coprime \(k(GV)\)-problem by controlling the numbers of conjugacy classes of stabilizers \(G_\lambda\) of \(G\)-orbits on \(\operatorname{Irr}(V)\), or equivalently on the dual module of \(V\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
